newsitem.title: INDIA: India faithful rush for last view of Gandhi ashes.
newsitem.headline: India faithful rush for last view of Gandhi ashes.

text.p: Hundreds of devotees of Mahatma Gandhi thronged to this sacred Hindu town in northern India on Wednesday for a last glimpse of a small wooden box holding the ashes of the independence leader.

Some authorities have called the claims that the ashes are Gandhi's a hoax, but many believe otherwise, and the saga of the simple urn containing the ashes appeared close to ending months after it began in a nondescript bank in southeastern India.

The ashes of Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi were due to arrive in Allahabad later on Wednesday by train. His relatives will immerse them at the Sangam, the confluence of three rivers -- the Yamuna, the Ganges and the mythical Saraswati.
"We have made all arrangements to pay due respects to the last remains of the father of the nation," Neeraj Gupta, Allahabad's district chief, told Reuters.

The wooden box on which India's eyes are riveted in the 50th year of independence from British rule was taken out on Tuesday to singing and ceremonial chants from the State Bank of India vault in the town of Cuttack in Orissa state by great-grandson Tushar Arun Gandhi.
After a fast -- Gandhi's favourite mode of protest -- and much media attention, the great-grandson won control in November of the box, which had lain in the vault since 1950.
The ashes travelled on a 19-hour train journey through four states to the banks of the Ganges, Hinduism's most sacred river, where they will be immersed on Thursday.
The day chosen for the immersion of the ashes was significant. January 30 is the 49th anniversary of the assassination of Gandhi by a Hindu fanatic.
The Mahatma, or great soul, as the leader was called, died only five months after India won independence from Britain.

He was cremated in Delhi, and his ashes were distributed across the nation for traditional immersions. The box in Cuttack, which bore the inscription "It contains the ashes of Mahatma Gandhi", lay forgotten until last year.

The ashes of Nathuram Godse, Gandhi's killer, have never been immersed. His relatives say he had wanted his remains to be scattered over the Indus river, which flows through what is now Pakistan, when it again becomes part of India.
Both Godse and Gandhi had opposed the partition of the subcontinent into India and Pakistan in 1947, although for different reasons.
Government officials in Allahabad were making feverish preparations to keep Gandhi's ashes in the government's Circuit House building.

The ashes will displayed for people to pay homage from 8.30 a.m (0300 GMT) on Thursday until 1 p.m. when the urn will be taken in a procession on a 10-km (six-mile) journey to the Sangam, officials said.
"In the wildest of my dreams, I never thought that I would be part of Bapuji's last rites," Gandhi's great grandson told Reuters on Tuesday, using a common term of endearment for the Mahatma.
The 38-year-old graphic artist said he was interested in entering politics.

"At the moment I cannot identify myself with any political party," he said. "I'm doing this immersion as a responsibility towards my great grandfather. I will not use Gandhi's name as an entry into politics."
